**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first word is always the hardest. It sits there, a tiny seed of sound, waiting to be planted in the soil of a sentence. But what if it’s the wrong one? What if the whole thing unravels before it even begins?

I used to think words were infinite, that they could stretch and bend to fit any shape I needed. But now I know they’re fragile. One misplaced syllable, one clumsy metaphor, and the whole structure collapses. Like a house of cards in a breeze.

II.

My grandmother’s hands were maps. Veins like rivers, knuckles like mountain ranges. She used to tell me stories about the old country—places I’d never seen, people I’d never meet. Her words were the only bridge between then and now.

Once, she described the taste of snow in winter: *"Like biting into a cloud, but colder."* I’ve never forgotten that. Words can be flavors. They can be textures. They can be the ghost of a sensation you’ve never felt.

III.

I read somewhere that the average person speaks about 16,000 words a day. Most of them are forgotten before they even leave the mouth. *"Pass the salt."* *"Did you take out the trash?"* *"I’m tired."*

But some words linger. The ones that cut. The ones that heal. The ones that sit in your chest like a stone.

IV.

There’s a word in Japanese—*komorebi*—that means the sunlight filtering through the leaves. English doesn’t have a word for that. We have to borrow it, like we’re stealing a little piece of beauty we didn’t know how to name.

What else are we missing? How many feelings do we carry around with no language to hold them?

V.

I once wrote a love letter I never sent. It was 372 words long. I counted. I thought if I could just get the words right, the feeling would be undeniable. But in the end, the words weren’t the problem. The problem was the silence after them.

VI.

The internet is a graveyard of words. Tweets, comments, status updates—millions of them, every second. Most will never be read. Most don’t deserve to be. But sometimes, in the noise, there’s a single sentence that makes you stop. Makes you *feel*.

I wonder how many masterpieces are lost in the scroll.

VII.

My father never said *"I love you."* Not in words. But he showed me how to fix a flat tire. How to build a fire. How to stand up straight when the world tries to knock you down.

Words aren’t the only language.

VIII.

I’m at 500 words now. Halfway. I could fill the rest with nonsense—random thoughts, half-formed ideas. But that feels like cheating.

Or maybe that’s the point. Maybe the best words are the ones that don’t try too hard. The ones that stumble out, messy and real.

IX.

I had a dream last night where I was drowning in a sea of letters. They swirled around me, forming and unforming, never quite making sense. I woke up gasping.

Sometimes words feel like that. Like they’re everywhere, but none of them are the right ones.

X.

There’s a quote—maybe it’s Hemingway, maybe it’s not—*"Write drunk, edit sober."* But what if you’re always a little bit of both? What if the words are always slightly blurred at the edges?

XI.

I think about the last words people say. The ones that get carved into history. *"Et tu, Brute?"* *"That’s one small step for man…"* *"I’ll be back."*

But most last words aren’t like that. Most are mundane. *"I’m thirsty."* *"Hold my hand."* *"Is it time?"*

Maybe the most important words are the quiet ones.

XII.

I’m at 800 words. The end is in sight. I could wrap this up neatly. Tie a bow on it. But I don’t want to.

Because the truth is, words don’t always have to mean something. Sometimes they just *are*. A pulse. A breath. A way to say, *"I was here."*

XIII.

The last word is the easiest. It’s the one that lets you walk away.

But I don’t want to walk away yet.

So I’ll leave it like this:

*(silence.)*
